candidates.title: Bone marrow stimulation improves 12-month clinical outcomes after isolated meniscal repair: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.
candidates.authors_short: Pakmanee N, Limitlaohaphan C, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare short-term clinical outcomes and meniscal healing on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 12 months between standard arthroscopic meniscal repair and repair augmented with bone marrow stimulation (BMS) in isolated meniscal tears. METHODS: In this prospective, two-centre, double-blind randomized controlled trial, patients aged 18-60 years with an isolated meniscal tear confirmed on MRI were randomized 1:1 to standard repair or repair augmented with BMS. Medial, lateral and bicompartmental tears were included. The primary outcome was the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score at 12 months. Secondary outcomes were the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Lysholm score, Tegner activity scale, pain on a visual analogue scale (VAS), patient satisfaction, operative time, adverse events and meniscal healing on 12-month MRI (3.0-T) (Crues classification, two-blinded assessors). RESULTS: Fifty patients (mean age 40.2 years; 21 male and 29 female) were randomized; all completed follow-up. Baseline characteristics were balanced; the augmented group received significantly more sutures (4.2 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1; p = 0.011) and had fewer horizontal tears (44% vs. 76%; p = 0.042). At 6 months, Lysholm and satisfaction scores already favoured the augmented group. At 12 months, it was superior for the IKDC score (82.5 ± 12.6 vs. 56.5 ± 18.5), WOMAC score (14.6 ± 20.0 vs. 41.8 ± 32.5), Lysholm score (91.8 ± 6.4 vs. 72.6 ± 17.2), Tegner activity scale (median 5.0, interquartile range [IQR] 4.0-6.0 vs. 3.0, IQR 2.0-4.0), pain (0.6 ± 0.7 vs. 2.3 ± 2.3) and satisfaction (9.7 ± 0.6 vs. 7.9 ± 1.7); all p < 0.05. MRI healing did not differ between groups (p = 0.783; unhealed: 2/25 [8%] per group); operative time was similar, and no complications occurred within 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, BMS augmentation was associated with superior patient-reported outcomes at 12 months, without additional complications or an increase in operative time. Meniscal healing on MRI did not differ between groups. These positive short-term findings helped to prove the benefit of BMS augmentation, although confirmation in larger trials with longer follow-up and structural assessment is required to clarify the effectiveness, durability and indications of BMS. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic randomized controlled trial.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality double-blind RCT from KSSTA showing bone marrow stimulation significantly improves 12-month outcomes after isolated meniscal repair, with large clinically meaningful effect sizes directly applicable to sports medicine practice.
bullets: Adding bone marrow stimulation to meniscal repair produced significantly better pain, function, and activity scores at 12 months compared to repair alone in adults aged 18 to 60 with isolated meniscal tears.
MRI healing rates were identical between groups at 12 months, suggesting the functional benefit from bone marrow stimulation is not explained by improved structural healing on imaging.
The technique added no extra operative time and no complications, making it a low-risk adjunct to consider for isolated meniscal repair pending confirmation in larger, longer studies.

candidates.title: Effect of Excision of the Infrapatellar Fat Pad in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Howard A, Naeem H, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is frequently excised during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) to improve exposure, but its role in postoperative pain and function is uncertain. Previous randomized trials and meta-analyses are equivocal, with follow-up limited to 12 months. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, participant- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. A total of 181 patients undergoing elective primary TKA for osteoarthritis were randomized intraoperatively to fat pad excision (removed) or minimal resection (retained). Implants and rehabilitation were standardized. The primary outcome was the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months; the secondary outcome was the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) at three, 12, and 24 months. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U-tests, and within-group changes over time using Kruskal-Wallis tests. In total, 140 participants were analyzed at 24 months (74 removed, 66 retained; 22% loss to follow-up). RESULTS: Both groups improved significantly across all KOOS subscales and OKS over time (P-values < 0.05), with gains exceeding the minimal clinically important difference on KOOS Pain. There were no significant between-group differences in KOOS or OKS at any time point (P-values > 0.05). The only within-group gain unique to one arm was KOOS Symptoms in the removed group between three and 24 months (P-values < 0.05). The KOOS scores did not improve between 12 and 24 months. CONCLUSION: In this study, excision or preservation of the fat pad did not significantly influence pain or function at two years postoperatively. The absence of change beyond 12 months suggests future trials could shorten follow-up.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT published in CORR from a high-impact journal comparing anterior vs posterolateral approach for THA with robust methodology (n=128), directly addressing one of the most debated questions in hip arthroplasty and finding no meaningful difference.
bullets: Removing or preserving the infrapatellar fat pad during primary TKA produced no difference in pain or function scores at two years.

Both groups improved beyond the minimum clinically important threshold for pain, meaning the fat pad decision does not appear to affect patient-reported outcomes in osteoarthritis patients undergoing elective TKA.
Scores plateaued after 12 months in both groups, so surgeons can reasonably use one-year follow-up as the endpoint in future fat pad trials.

candidates.title: No Differences in Patient-reported Outcomes Between the Direct Anterior and Posterolateral Approach for THA: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Rykov K, de Vries AJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The direct anterior approach (DAA) for THA is seeing wider use because it is purported to deliver a faster postoperative recovery. However, most previous studies comparing the DAA with the posterolateral approach (PLA) were limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous patient populations, and the use of outcome measures with ceiling effects. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does the DAA result in a higher proportion of patients achieving the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) on the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) after THA compared with the PLA? (2) Are there differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, health-related quality of life (QoL), or complications between the DAA and PLA in the first postoperative year? METHODS: A prospective, parallel-group, nonblinded, randomized controlled trial comparing the DAA and PLA for THA was conducted. Patients with primary or secondary osteoarthritis with an indication for THA with an uncemented femoral stem and cemented acetabular component were eligible. Of the 241 patients assessed for eligibility, 53% (128) were included in the study. Fifty-one percent (65 of 128) were randomized to the DAA group, and 49% (63 of 128) were randomized to the PLA group. One patient in each group was lost to follow-up, leaving 98% (64 of 65) and 98% (62 of 63) of patients available for analysis, respectively. There were no between-group differences in baseline or perioperative measurements. The primary outcome was achievement of the PASS on the HOOS at 3 months postoperatively. An a priori sample-size calculation indicated that 60 patients per group were required to detect a 20% difference in PASS achievement between groups (80% power; α = 0.05). With an expected loss to follow-up of 10%, the sample size was set to 65 patients per group. Secondary outcomes included symptoms, physical functioning, participation, and health-related QoL, assessed using patient-reported outcome measures and physical performance tests. Complications were assessed using the Clavien-Dindo classification. Outcomes were assessed preoperatively as well as at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year postoperatively. RESULTS: At 3 months, the proportion of patients achieving the PASS did not differ between the DAA and PLA for any HOOS subscales, including symptoms (65% [41 of 63] versus 63% [39 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.80 to 1.35]; p = 0.80), pain (48% [30 of 63] versus 53% [33 of 62], OR 0.90 [95% CI 0.63 to 1.27]; p = 0.53), activities of daily living (68% [43 of 63] versus 65% [40 of 62], OR 1.06 [95% CI 0.82 to 1.36]; p = 0.66), sports and recreation (55% [34 of 62] versus 58% [36 of 62], OR 0.94 [95% CI 0.69 to 1.29]; p = 0.72), and QoL (73% [46 of 63] versus 71% [44 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% CI 0.83 to 1.28]; p = 0.80). There were no between-group differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, and health-related QoL at any time point. Complications occurred in 8% (5 of 65) of patients in the DAA group and 2% (1 of 63) of patients in the PLA group (OR 3.05 [95% CI 0.51 to 18.40]; p = 0.21). CONCLUSION: In this randomized controlled trial, the DAA did not improve patient-reported or functional outcomes compared with the PLA during the first postoperative year. In the absence of demonstrated patient-reported or functional benefits of the DAA, surgeons should not represent to patients that the DAA provides advantages in terms of the pace or magnitude of recovery. Future studies powered to detect differences in the risk of complications should be performed to see whether harms are more likely with the DAA than with other surgical approaches. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT in Journal of Arthroplasty evaluating fat pad excision during TKA with 181 patients and 24-month follow-up, providing Level I evidence for a common intraoperative decision with clear practice implications.
bullets: In this RCT of 126 THA patients, the direct anterior approach produced no difference in pain, function, or quality of life compared to the posterolateral approach at any point through one year.
These findings apply to patients undergoing primary THA, meaning surgeons should not tell patients the anterior approach offers a faster or better recovery.
Complication rates trended higher in the anterior approach group (8% vs 2%), supporting a need for larger studies to clarify whether the approach carries added risk.

candidates.title: Patient Profile and Cause-Specific Lifetime Revision Risk of Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty: An Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry Study.
candidates.authors_short: Rele S, Zhou Y, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Traditional estimates of implant survival reported by joint registries neglect to account for a person's remaining life expectancy after arthroplasty. This study aimed to estimate lifetime revision risk for primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA) across different patient profiles using a large, national joint replacement registry. METHODS: All patients undergoing primary TKA for osteoarthritis from the Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2020, were included. Patients were organized into 5-year age bands at the time of TKA, and the cumulative lifetime revision risk was calculated, stratified by patient sex, body mass index, American Society of Anesthesiology scores, and causes of revision. RESULTS: The highest lifetime revision rate was observed in the youngest, 46- to 50-year-old age group (39.0%, 95% confidence interval (CI), 38.3 to 39.8), decreasing to 0% in the 96- to 100-year-old group. Men were associated with higher lifetime revision risk from the 46- to 50-year old group (41.7%, 95% CI, 40.4 to 43.0; women: 37.0%, 95% CI, 36.2 to 37.9). Morbid obesity was associated with higher lifetime revision risk until 80 years of age (76 to 80 years: 5.2%, 95% CI, 3.6 to 6.8). American Society of Anesthesiology class 4 was associated with the highest lifetime revision risk until age 65 years (61 to 65: 12.2%, 95% CI, 9.3 to 15.2). At all ages, infection had the highest lifetime revision risk. CONCLUSION: Lifetime revision risk provides an easier-to-understand metric for the risk of revision for patients. This study shows lifetime revision risk is highest among young men.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large national registry study from JBJS-level journal (JAAOS) using Australian registry data to quantify lifetime revision risk for primary TKA stratified by patient profile, providing directly actionable counseling data.
bullets: Young patients aged 46 to 50 facing total knee replacement carry a nearly 40% lifetime revision risk, with young men at the highest risk of all groups.
Morbid obesity raises lifetime revision risk up to age 80, and infection is the leading cause of revision across every age group.
Lifetime revision risk, rather than traditional implant survival curves, gives patients and surgeons a more intuitive basis for shared decision making before primary TKA.

candidates.title: Evolving Management of Hip Fracture Patients on Anticoagulant and Antiplatelet Medications: A 22-Year Cohort Study.
candidates.authors_short: House HE, Schwartz A, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate temporal trends in anticoagulant (AC) and antiplatelet (AP) use among patients undergoing operative treatment of hip fractures and to assess the association of antithrombotic regimen with time to surgery and postoperative outcomes. METHODS: Design: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Single North American Level I trauma center. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged 55 years or older who underwent operative treatment for a hip fracture (AO/OTA types 31-A, 31-B, and 31-C) between 2000 and 2022 while receiving anticoagulant and/or antiplatelet therapy at admission were included. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Temporal trends in antithrombotic prescribing, time to surgery, perioperative transfusion, readmission, 90-day medical and surgical postoperative complications, and 90-day mortality were assessed. The odds of warfarin versus direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) prescription were compared across study years, and time to surgery from admission and each outcome were compared across study years and across antithrombotic regimens (warfarin, DOAC, DOAC or warfarin plus antiplatelet, and antiplatelet alone). RESULTS: 476 patients were included (mean age 81.2 years [range, 60-103]; 288 [60.4%] female). Anticoagulant therapy was used by 155 (32.7%) and antiplatelet therapy by 385 (80.7%); 64 (13.4%) received both. The odds of warfarin prescription relative to a DOAC decreased by an estimated 37% per year (odds ratio [OR] 0.63, 95% CI 0.53-0.74; P<0.001). Time to surgery did not change significantly over the study period (-0.01 hours/year, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.02; P=0.4) and was not associated with antithrombotic regimen (-0.01, 95% CI: -0.04-0.01; P=0.3). Perioperative transfusion odds decreased 12% per year (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.84-0.93; P<0.001) and 1-year readmission odds decreased 46% per year (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.48-0.60; P<0.001), independent of medication class. Ninety-day (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.04; P=0.8) and 90-day mortality (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.54-1.14; P=0.2) did not change over time. CONCLUSIONS: In this 22-year single-center cohort of hip-fracture patients receiving anticoagulant (AC) or antiplatelet (AP) therapy, antithrombotic regimen was not associated with time to surgery, 90-day complications, or mortality. Perioperative transfusion and 1-year readmission rates declined over the study period independent of medication class. These findings supported expedited operative management of hip fractures in patients receiving AC or AP therapy. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.
candidates.score_reasoning: 22-year retrospective cohort of 476 hip fracture patients on anticoagulants/antiplatelets documenting the DOAC transition and outcomes, highly relevant to daily trauma practice managing this common and complex perioperative scenario.
bullets: In hip fracture patients over 55 on anticoagulants or antiplatelets, the specific medication class did not affect time to surgery, 90-day complications, or mortality.
Perioperative transfusion rates and one-year readmission rates both declined significantly over 22 years, independent of which antithrombotic the patient was taking.
These findings support proceeding to surgery without delay in hip fracture patients on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, regardless of the specific agent.

candidates.title: Does the Timing of Surgical Debridement Affect Outcomes in Septic Arthritis of the Native Hip and Knee? A Propensity-weighted Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Randall ZD, Barber HF, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Septic arthritis of the native hip and knee can cause irreversible cartilage damage and systemic illness. Because operative debridement provides source control, delaying it may permit infection to progress, potentially increasing the need for repeat surgery and the risk of death; however, evidence examining these associations remains limited. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: Is delayed debridement associated with increased risk of (1) repeat debridement or (2) 1-year mortality in septic arthritis of the native hip and/or knee? METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the Florida State Inpatient Database, a statewide, all-payer database that records procedures by hospital day and includes longitudinal patient identifiers. Between October 2015 and December 2022, we identified 3587 adult admissions involving septic arthritis of the native hip (n = 1014) or knee (n = 2573) treated with surgical debridement. We excluded 1% (42 of 3587) of admitted patients in whom the first debridement occurred after hospital day 10, leaving 99% (3545 of 3587) for analysis (hip n = 1001; knee n = 2544). No included outcome or covariate data were missing. In the screened hip and knee cohorts, the mean ± SD ages were 55 ± 17 years and 60 ± 16 years, respectively, and 46% (462 of 1014) and 34% (879 of 2573) were female. Debridement occurred on hospital days 0 to 1 in 51% (506 of 1001) of hip admissions and 59% (1510 of 2544) of knee admissions; the remaining 49% (495 of 1001) and 41% (1034 of 2544), respectively, underwent debridement on day 2 or later. Stabilized inverse probability-of-treatment weighting was used to balance measured baseline covariates. Weighted log-binomial regression was used to estimate adjusted relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Among patients with septic knee arthritis, debridement on day 2 or later was associated with a higher risk of repeat debridement than debridement on days 0 to 1 (13% [133 of 1034] versus 5% [72 of 1510], adjusted RR 2.40 [95% CI 1.81 to 3.19]; p < 0.001). One-year mortality also was higher after debridement on day 2 or later (11% [118 of 1034] versus 6% [88 of 1510], adjusted RR 1.54 [95% CI 1.17 to 2.02]; p = 0.002). Among patients with septic hip arthritis, repeat debridement was no different between those treated on day 2 or later and those treated on days 0 to 1 (11% [55 of 495] versus 7% [37 of 506], adjusted RR 1.43 [95% CI 0.95 to 2.15]; p = 0.09). One-year mortality also was no different between the hip timing groups (9% [43 of 495] versus 7% [35 of 506], adjusted RR 1.19 [95% CI 0.77 to 1.85]; p = 0.44). CONCLUSION: Surgeons should prioritize prompt debridement of septic knee arthritis, and hospitals should implement coordinated pathways to avoid preventable delays. No timing-specific recommendation can be made for septic hip arthritis based on our findings. Larger multicenter studies with granular data on presentation, diagnostic aspiration, antibiotic administration, and debridement are needed to clarify whether debridement timing influences outcomes in septic hip arthritis and to distinguish preventable delays from those related to diagnostic uncertainty or the management of medical comorbidities. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT from CORR comparing debridement timing in native hip and knee septic arthritis using propensity-weighted analysis of 3545 patients, directly addressing a critical and time-sensitive clinical decision.
bullets: In septic knee arthritis, delaying surgical debridement to day 2 or later more than doubled the risk of repeat surgery and increased one-year mortality compared to debridement within the first two days.
No significant difference in repeat debridement or one-year mortality was found based on timing of debridement in septic hip arthritis.
Orthopaedic surgeons should treat septic knee arthritis as a time-sensitive emergency and work with hospitals to remove avoidable delays to the operating room.

candidates.title: Tranexamic Acid Administration is Associated With Lower Transfusion Rates and Wound Complications Following Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty for Periprosthetic Joint Infection.
candidates.authors_short: Kumaran P, Wier J, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tranexamic acid (TXA) is widely used in total joint arthroplasty, but data on its efficacy in periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) of the knee are scarce. We assessed TXA efficacy in revision total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for PJI. METHODS: A national database was queried for patients ≥18 years undergoing stage-one revision TKA for PJI from 2016 to 2023. Patients with and without TXA exposure were propensity matched. Multivariable logistic regression assessed primary outcomes (postoperative transfusion, bleeding complications, and wound complications) and secondary outcomes (thromboembolic complications). RESULTS: Overall, 13,247 TXA patients were matched 1:1 to 13,247 non-TXA patients on comorbidities, Charlson Comorbidity Index, demographics, hospital characteristics, and preoperative transfusion rates, all with standardized mean differences <0.10. Mean age was 67.4 years in both cohorts, with similar use of venous thromboembolic chemoprophylaxis. TXA was associated with decreased adjusted odds of postoperative transfusion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.69-0.85, P < .001) and aggregate wound complications (aOR: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.60-0.70, P < .001), with similar odds of aggregate bleeding complications (aOR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.95-1.09, P = .563). Odds of aggregate venous thromboembolism (aOR: 0.97, 95% CI: 0.82-1.13, P = .874), deep vein thrombosis (aOR: 1.00, 95% CI: 1.00-1.01, P = .309), and pulmonary embolism (aOR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.83-1.34, P = .639) were similar. CONCLUSIONS: TXA was associated with lower rates of transfusion and aggregate wound complications, without increased venous thromboembolism risk, during revision TKA for PJI.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large propensity-matched database study of TXA use in revision TKA for PJI (n=26,494), providing strong evidence supporting TXA in this high-stakes setting where data were previously scarce.
bullets: TXA use in revision knee arthroplasty for periprosthetic joint infection reduced transfusion rates and wound complications without increasing clot risk.
These findings apply to adult patients undergoing first-stage revision for knee PJI, a population historically excluded from most TXA efficacy data.
Surgeons should not withhold TXA in PJI revision cases out of concern for thromboembolism, as rates were equivalent to non-TXA patients.

candidates.title: Local Bone Density of Preoperative CT: A Predictor of Clinically Significant Shortening and Varus Collapse of Well-Reduced Geriatric Intertrochanteric Hip Fractures.
candidates.authors_short: Kashyap J, Kuhn MZ, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Intertrochanteric (IT) fractures are the most common geriatric hip fracture, with early fixation failure contributing to high morbidity and mortality. Lower bone density, as measured by Hounsfield units (HU) from CT scans, is predictive of various long bone fractures and fracture fixation failure, although its role in IT fractures is less well described. We aimed to assess the association between local bone density and radiographic outcomes after cephalomedullary nail (CMN) fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, hypothesizing that lower HU measurements are associated with increased rates of clinically significant shortening and varus collapse. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients older than 60 years with low-energy IT fractures treated with a long or short CMN between 2017 and 2024 at a single institution. Fractures with varus malreduction or tip apex distance >25 mm were excluded. Radiographs were assessed postoperatively and at 6 to 24-week follow-up to evaluate for shortening and change in the neck-shaft angle. Hounsfield unit measurements of the proximal femur were obtained from injury CT scans. Two-sample t-tests, simple linear regression, and multivariate logistic regression were used to analyze the relationship between HU and shortening/varus collapse. RESULTS: Among 103 patients (74 women, 29 men; mean age 79.3 ± 9.8 years), the mean local bone density was 193.3 ± 63.4 HU. Patients with clinically significant shortening or varus collapse (n = 38) had significantly lower HU than those without (n = 65) (160.9 vs. 212.3 HU, P < 0.0001). HU was independently associated with shortening/varus collapse (OR 0.98, P < 0.01) and negatively correlated with magnitude of shortening (R2 = 0.091, P < 0.01). An exploratory threshold of 150 HU significantly predicted shortening. CONCLUSIONS: Lower local bone density predicts shortening/varus collapse after CMN fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, despite optimization of modifiable surgical factors. An exploratory threshold of 150 HU may identify patients at risk of shortening within 24 weeks postoperatively.
candidates.score_reasoning: JAAOS study using CT-derived Hounsfield units to predict fixation failure after intertrochanteric fracture nail fixation, offering a novel preoperative risk stratification tool with immediate clinical utility.
bullets: In geriatric intertrochanteric fractures fixed with a cephalomedullary nail, patients who developed shortening or varus collapse had meaningfully lower proximal femur bone density on CT than those who did not (161 vs. 212 Hounsfield units).
A preoperative CT Hounsfield unit threshold of 150 identified patients at elevated risk for clinically significant shortening within 24 weeks, even after well-reduced, well-implanted fixation.

For orthopaedic surgeons treating elderly hip fracture patients, routine CT Hounsfield unit measurement offers a practical, no-cost tool to flag high-risk patients for closer postoperative monitoring or augmented fixation strategies.

candidates.title: Functional outcomes over 24 months after arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tendon tears in a multicentre study.
candidates.authors_short: Audigé L, Croci E, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Isolated subscapularis tears are rare, and it is currently unclear how the tear size relates to the postoperative outcomes after arthroscopic repair. This study aimed to evaluate clinical- and patient-reported outcomes, as well as adverse events of arthroscopically treated isolated subscapularis tears based on the tear extent over 24 months. METHODS: Across 19 orthopaedic centres, 69 patients undergoing primary arthroscopic repair for isolated subscapularis tears were prospectively recruited between June 2020 and November 2021. Medical imaging examinations were conducted at baseline and at 12 months. Clinical- and patient-reported outcomes were obtained at baseline, 6, 12, and 24 months. Adverse events within 24 months were documented. Patients were grouped into partial tears (n = 14), full-thickness tears of the superior half (n = 35) or complete full-thickness tears (n = 20) of the subscapularis. All outcomes were compared using generalised linear mixed models adjusted for baseline values, age, sex, American Society of Anaesthesiologists classification, tear aetiology, and steroid infiltrations. RESULTS: Improvements in all outcome scores were observed after surgery. No group differences were observed in the ranges of motion in flexion, abduction and external rotation (P≥0.634). The partial tear group had a higher pain level than both full-thickness groups at 12 months (P≤0.005). Abduction strength, Constant Score, Oxford Shoulder Score, Subjective Shoulder Value and EQ-5D-5L showed positive changes within 12- or 24-month follow-ups, with no group differences (P≥0.089). The risk of at least a symptomatic adverse event of any severity level affecting the operated shoulder and arm was highest for patients with partial tears (50%) and lowest for patients with complete full-thickness tears (25%). The most frequent occurrences were persistent or worsening pain, stiffness, and recurrent defects. Overall, 62% of patients with partial tears, 97% of patients with superior full-thickness tears and 77% of patients with complete full-thickness tears were satisfied at 24 months. CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tears leads to significant and sustained improvements in clinical and patient-reported outcomes over 24 months, regardless of tear extent. However, patients with partial tears demonstrated greater residual pain and fewer patients reported satisfaction compared with those with full-thickness tears. These findings may reflect differences in patient characteristics and surgical treatment choices. Further studies are needed to determine the suitability and efficacy of surgical treatments for isolated subscapularis partial tears. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison, Prognosis Study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Registry-based cohort study from Dutch Arthroplasty Register (n=1,683) examining glenohumeral radial mismatch and glenoid loosening in aTSA, providing important implant selection guidance with strong methodology.
bullets: Arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tears improves strength, range of motion, and patient-reported scores by 24 months regardless of whether the tear is partial or full-thickness.
Patients with partial subscapularis tears had more residual pain, more adverse events, and lower satisfaction at 24 months compared to those with full-thickness tears.
Surgeons should counsel patients with partial subscapularis tears that outcomes after repair are less predictable than for full-thickness tears, and the role of surgery in this group remains unclear.

candidates.title: Risk of Venous Thromboembolism After Lumbar Spine Interbody Fusion: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.
candidates.authors_short: Silvestre J, Ferdon RJ, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a feared complication after spine surgery, with limited data comparing approach-specific risk factors after lumbar interbody fusion. This study compared the rate of VTE complications after transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) and anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF). METHODS: A multi-institutional electronic medical record database was queried for patients aged older than 18 years undergoing single-level or multilevel TLIF and ALIF between 2004 and 2024. Patients were evenly divided into single-level (n = 9,618) and multilevel (n = 1,774) TLIF and ALIF cohorts. Propensity score matching (1:1) was conducted using demographics, comorbidities, and anticoagulation use. Odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) of VTE and postoperative bleeding complications were calculated at 30, 60, and 90 days. RESULTS: Compared with single-level TLIF, single-level ALIF was associated with higher odds of VTE events at 30 days (OR: 2.0, 95% CI, 1.4 to 2.9; P < 0.001), 60 days (OR: 1.8, 95% CI, 1.3 to 2.5; P < 0.001), and 90 days (OR: 1.7, 95% CI, 1.3 to 2.4; P < 0.001). Multilevel ALIF was also associated with higher odds of VTE events at 30 days (OR: 2.7, 95% CI: 1.2 to 5.1; P = 0.015), 60 days (OR: 2.0, 95% CI, 1.2 to 3.4; P = 0.010), and 90 days (OR: 1.9, 95% CI, 1.1 to 3.2; P = 0.015) when compared with multilevel TLIF. No significant differences were observed in postoperative bleeding complications between single-level and multilevel TLIF and ALIF cohorts at all study intervals (P > 0.05). DISCUSSION: ALIF was associated with increased VTE complications, with no differences in postoperative bleeding complications when compared with TLIF. These findings suggest that surgical approach should be considered in perioperative VTE risk stratification and patient counseling after lumbar interbody fusion surgery, highlighting the need for future prospective studies evaluating approach-specific VTE prevention strategies.

bullets: ALIF carries roughly twice the VTE risk of TLIF at 30, 60, and 90 days, for both single-level and multilevel cases.
Postoperative bleeding rates were similar between ALIF and TLIF, so more aggressive prophylaxis after ALIF does not appear to trade in higher bleeding risk.
Surgical approach should be factored into perioperative VTE counseling and prophylaxis planning for any patient scheduled for lumbar interbody fusion.
